Stage 01

Pre-Incorporation & Know-Your-Customer

UBO transparency, Apostille authentication chain, official name clearance restricted wordlist, and pre-incorporation statutory fee budget.

UBO Ultimate Beneficial Owner Screening Rules Official Registry Only

>=25% ownership / control

Applicable AML statute: Ley 10/2010, de 28 de abril, de prevención del blanqueo de capitales y de la financiación del terrorismo, as amended by Ley 6/2023 (transposing AMLD5) and developed by Real Decreto 304/2014; UBO transparency registers (Registro de Titularidades Reales) governed by Real Decreto 609/2023, de 11 de julio; corporate incorporation governed by Real Decreto Legislativo 1/2010 (Ley de Sociedades de Capital); name clearance governed by Reglamento del Registro Mercantil (RRM), Articles 403–414.
Registered Agent & Physical Address Licensed Agent Required

Virtual offices are acknowledged for SL e-commerce structures provided the registered address serves as a genuine communication hub where official notifications (AEAT tax notices, Registro Mercantil correspondence, and judicial service) can be physically received and forwarded. For the online jewellery and fine timepieces segment, a purely letterbox address without any operational capacity is discouraged because Spanish customs (Agencia Tributaria – Departamento de Aduanas) and platform payment processors (Stripe/PayPal) may demand evidence of a real establishment, VAT registration address consistency, and returns-management capability. Industry-accepted practice: a serviced office with administrative reception, mail handling, and records custody for a minimum of 12 months satisfies current substance v. letterbox scrutiny at Stage 1.

✓ Partner licensed company-secretary channels provide local registered address and government mail forwarding.

Stage 02

Statutory Formation & Board Resolutions

Competent registry, governing statute, capital lockup rules, and first board resolution template.

Competent corporate registry

Registro Mercantil Central (Central Commercial Registry, Madrid) for the corporate name certificate; Registro Mercantil Provincial of the province of the registered office for the statutory inscription (e.g., Registro Mercantil de Madrid).

Governing statute

Royal Legislative Decree 1/2010 of 2 July approving the consolidated text of the Spanish Capital Companies Act (Ley de Sociedades de Capital - LSC), Title II (Arts. 19-22: incorporation deed, registration, legal personality), Art. 4 (minimum capital), Chapters on the Management Body (Arts. 209-212); Royal Decree 1784/1996 (Reglamento del Registro Mercantil) and Commercial Code Arts. 119-124.

Formation / constitutional filings

Public deed of incorporation (Escritura de Constitución) granted before a Spanish notary, followed by an application for inscription (inscripción) in the Provincial Mercantile Registry.

Incorporation processing time

⚡ 33 business days (SOP sum)

Paid-up Capital & Blocked Account Regime Mandatory Capital Deposit & Lockup

Minimum share capital of EUR 3,000 (Art. 4 LSC) fully subscribed and fully paid up at constitution; the funds must be deposited in a blocked 'company in formation' bank account in a Spanish credit institution and evidenced by a bank certificate (certificado bancario de desembolso) attached to the deed, or substituted by a notarial deposit certificate or an expert report for non-cash contributions.

Funding & unlock path: Fire safety compliance under Royal Decree 513/2017 (Reglamento de instalaciones de protección contra incendios) with the municipal fire certification for the premises; structural and electrical safety inspections for the registered office/warehouse; occupational risk prevention plan and health surveillance under Ley 31/1995 (PRL) with a preventive service; workplace first-aid and emergency equipment; the company is not subject to the Seveso III major-accident duties due to the low-risk retail activity.

Paid-in capital rule: Minimum share capital of EUR 3,000 (Art. 4 LSC) fully subscribed and fully paid up at constitution; the funds must be deposited in a blocked 'company in formation' bank account in a Spanish credit institution and evidenced by a bank certificate (certificado bancario de desembolso) attached to the deed, or substituted by a notarial deposit certificate or an expert report for non-cash contributions.

Industrial Access / EIA & Civil Defense Approval Exempted / Not Required

Ayuntamiento de Madrid (Municipal authority - Área de Gobierno de Medio Ambiente y Movilidad) for the municipal opening communication and premises compliance; for precious metal articles, the Centro Español de Metrología (CEM) and the competent hallmarking bodies under Ley 3/1992.

Category: Not required - online retail of jewelry, watches and fashion accessories (ISIC 4791) has no sector-specific industrial operating permit. Where physical premises (warehouse/office) are opened, a municipal 'Comunicación Previa de Apertura' or 'Licencia de Actividad' may apply under Ley 12/2012 on simplified licensing; compliance with Ley 3/1992 (hallmarking rules for articles containing precious metals) is required only if such articles are sold.

Stage 03

Tax Identity & Indirect Tax

Tax authority e-portal, entity tax classification elections, VAT thresholds, and 0% export documentation chain.

Tax ID Application Infrastructure

Competent tax authority

Agencia Estatal de Administración Tributaria (AEAT) - Sede Electrónica: https://sede.agenciatributaria.gob.es

E-government filing portal

A foreign investor incorporating a Spanish SL obtains a provisional NIF from the AEAT immediately after execution of the public deed and registration in the Mercantile Registry, then files Form 036 before the start of any economic activity to receive the definitive NIF and declare the IVA and IAE census status. A non-resident entity supplying goods or services in Spain without a permanent establishment must apply for a Non-Resident NIF (NIF-NR) on Form 030 before the first supply and appoint a Spanish fiscal representative if AEAT so requires. A Spanish branch or permanent establishment of the foreign parent applies for its own NIF on Form 036, annexing the parent's certificate of tax residence, constitution documents, and board resolution appointing the permanent establishment representative. The same NIF is used for IS, IVA, customs, statistical, and payroll purposes.

Tax ID type & application path: Entity_Level_Taxation — A foreign investor incorporating a Spanish SL obtains a provisional NIF from the AEAT immediately after execution of the public deed and registration in the Mercantile Registry, then files Form 036 before the start of any economic activity to receive the definitive NIF and declare the IVA and IAE census status. A non-resident entity supplying goods or services in Spain without a permanent establishment must apply for a Non-Resident NIF (NIF-NR) on Form 030 before the first supply and appoint a Spanish fiscal representative if AEAT so requires. A Spanish branch or permanent establishment of the foreign parent applies for its own NIF on Form 036, annexing the parent's certificate of tax residence, constitution documents, and board resolution appointing the permanent establishment representative. The same NIF is used for IS, IVA, customs, statistical, and payroll purposes.

Default Tax Classification & Elections

Default tax classification

Entity_Level_Taxation

Available election forms

Spain does not provide a US-style check-the-box or pass-through election. An SL is irrevocably a resident capital company taxable under Impuesto sobre Sociedades at entity level. Optional elections relevant to the same structure include the Spanish group consolidation regime for groups that satisfy the voting thresholds (article 64 LIS), the ETVE holding-company regime for eligible Spanish holding entities only, and ordinary elections such as the simplified cash-basis IVA regime for small SMEs. Hybrid mismatch positions are strictly governed by ATAD transposition under LIS articles 15oct, 15non and 15decies; no unilateral hybrid election is permitted, and taxpayers must document any cross-border instrument with the tax file to prevent deduction/non-inclusion mismatches.

VAT / GST & 0% Export Zero-Rating

Standard VAT / GST rate

21%

Mandatory registration threshold (Nexus)

No general de minimis threshold: any taxable economic activity in Spain requires IVA registration on the Census of Entrepreneurs, Professionals and Withholders before commencement. For a non-established e-commerce operator, registration is triggered by the first importation or first supply located in Spain; the EUR 10,000 pan-EU distance-sales threshold is an EU OSS routing rule and not a Spanish VAT registration exemption once goods are in or imported into Spain.

Export 0% zero-rating conditions

A Spanish exporter of jewelry, watches, and fashion goods may apply a 0% IVA rate as an export (exempt with credit of input VAT under article 21 LIVA) if the goods are physically dispatched or transported to a non-EU destination by the seller, purchaser, or a third party, normally within three months of the supply, and if the customs export declaration is accepted by Spanish Customs. The exporter must prove the exit from EU customs territory by transport documentation and keep the export evidence in the accounting file. Intra-EU B2B dispatches to a customer with a valid EU VAT number are zero-rated under article 25 LIVA, supported by the customer's VAT number, transport evidence, and recapitulative statement Model 349. Ancillary freight and loading services physically performed in Spain on exported goods are exempt. Digital or offshore services to non-EU business customers are generally outside the scope of Spanish IVA under the place-of-supply rules and do not require a 0% rate, but must be documented by contract, customer residence/establishment evidence, and bank payment records; input VAT on costs directly attributable to exported or outside-scope supplies can be deducted to the extent allowed by pro-rata rules.

  • Customs Export Declaration (Single Administrative Document / e-DUA) accepted and released by Spanish Customs in the Export Control System (ECS), showing the third-country destination and export customs number
  • Bill of Lading, Air Waybill, or CMR transport document evidencing physical exit of the goods from the EU customs territory to the non-EU country, including consignee details, loading date, and port/airport of departure
  • Inward Remittance Certificate (SWIFT MT103 or bank-signed certificate of payment) proving receipt and repatriation of the export consideration from the foreign buyer to the Spanish exporter

Spain does not operate an Italian-style real-time fiscal clearing stamp (cAI). Instead: (1) large taxpayers in the SII (Suministro Inmediato de Información) regime - annual IVA turnover exceeding EUR 6,000,000 or consolidated groups returning monthly IVA - transmit invoice and transaction registers to AEAT through secured web services within 4 calendar days of accrual or invoice issuance; (2) Royal Decree 1007/2023 implementing Law 18/2022 (Crea y Crece) mandates software and electronic invoicing standards (Facturae format) for B2B invoices and Verifactu-compliant billing software, with phased enforceability from 2024-2025; (3) invoices to public authorities are submitted through the FACe platform in Facturae XML; (4) online jewelry/watches sellers must maintain interoperable e-invoice repositories and expose transaction dates, counterpart NIF/NIF-NR, amounts, and export customs numbers to AEAT on request; there is no AEAT pre-clearance or digital stamp per invoice.

AEAT automatically cross-validates customs exit declarations (ECS), VAT returns (Model 303/390), marketplace seller reports from OSS, and inbound payment flows (SWIFT MT103) through its data warehouse. If the export zero-rating is not substantiated by the required customs and transport documents or if foreign proceeds are not repatriated within the 180-day benchmark, the exemption is denied retroactively and IVA is assessed at 21% on the invoiced amount, plus late-payment interest (interés de demora) and proportional penalties under LGT articles 191-193. The penalty scale is 50%-100% for negligent omission, 100%-150% for fraudulent under-declaration or suppression of records, and criminal tax prosecution (delito contra la Hacienda Pública) can apply if the defrauded annual tax amount exceeds EUR 120,000. Because jewelry and timepieces are high-value, low-volume goods, AEAT applies particularly intensive scrutiny to artificial triangular shipments, temporary imports re-exported without IVA, and payouts through PSPs not reconciled with the export declaration.

Stage 04

Banking & Treasury Architecture

Central-bank FX diagnosis, tier-1 local banks vs offshore digital EMI matrix, and KYC rejection defense guide.

Foreign Exchange Regime & Central Bank Policy

Current-account convertibility

Spain is a euro-area member and maintains no currency exchange controls: the euro is fully convertible, and both current-account flows (export/online-sale receipts, royalties, dividends, profit remittances) and capital-account flows (equity subscriptions, shareholder loans, liquidation proceeds) are liberalised under Articles 63 to 66 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union and Law 19/2003. Profit remittance to non-resident shareholders is unrestricted at the FX and treasury level; the only frictions are (i) Spanish tax withholding on distributions (19% general non-resident rate, reduced to 0% under the EU Parent-Subsidiary Directive or to the applicable treaty rate, usually 5-10%, under the relevant double-taxation treaty) and (ii) mandatory statistical and administrative filings to the Banco de España for resident/non-resident transactions reaching reporting thresholds: payment-service providers must capture transfer-level information for amounts equal to or greater than EUR 50,000; certain operations (for example external shareholder loans and guarantees) require an individual 'declaración de operación exterior' when the amount exceeds EUR 150,000; and an annual 'posición de activos y pasivos con no residentes' declaration applies when gross balances exceed EUR 1,000,000. The ISIC 4791 e-commerce jewellery/watch business is not in Spain's screened FDI sectors (defence, critical infrastructure, media, energy, personal-data platforms under Royal Decree-Law 8/2020 and 11/2020), so inbound equity and minority foreign ownership are fully admissible without prior authorisation, conversion, surrender, or licence burdens.

Export proceeds surrender rules

Spain repealed all export-proceeds surrender obligations upon full liberalisation of external transactions: exporters, including the SL's online jewellery/watch merchant, are not required to repatriate proceeds within any statutory deadline, are not compelled to convert receipts into euro, and may retain 100% of collections in foreign-currency settlement accounts or in Spanish-authorised e-money wallets. The mandatory nexus is documentation and statistics: (i) physical exportations are declared through the AEAT customs platform using the DUA/ECS (Export Control System) with a customs value consistent with the commercial invoice; (ii) intra-EU dispatches require Intrastat declarations annually when the dispatch value exceeds EUR 400,000; and (iii) every cross-border transfer executed via a Spanish intermediary is transmitted by that bank to the Banco de España balance-of-payments register when the amount meets the applicable capture threshold (EUR 50,000 per transfer; EUR 1,000,000 for gross position declarations). No conversion ratio, no foreign-exchange certificate, no central-bank authorisation of sales proceeds, and no penalty timeline apply beyond the standard AEAT VAT/CIT reporting calendar.

Central bank supervision: Banco de España (Bank of Spain); operational foreign-trade and investment statistics are administered jointly with the Secretaría de Estado de Comercio and the Dirección General de Comercio Internacional e Inversiones (DGCIIN) of the Ministry of Economy, Trade and Business, under Law 19/2003 of 4 July on Capital Movements and Economic Transactions and Royal Decree 1816/1991 of 28 December on Economic Transactions with the Exterior.

Offshore Digital Bank / EMI Whitelist

Cross-border EMI / Fintech rails Fit: High

Feasibility rating: MEDIUM-HIGH for Spanish-regulated electronic-money institutions and payment institutions (entidades de dinero electrónico/entidades de pago) holding a valid Banco de España licence (for example Monei, Bnext and RedSys-backed issuers); such domestic EMIs can lawfully provide IBANs, card acquiring, e-money floats and payout rails for the SL's e-commerce settlement. Their limitations are commercial rather than legal: they seldom offer meaningful FX lines, high-value watch-trade finance, commercial letters of credit, or the correspondent bank network of a tier-1 credit institution, so they should be used as secondary collection rails, not as the anchor treasury bank. Offshore digital EMIs (post-Brexit UK-licensed EMIs, Lithuanian, Polish, or other issuers without a branch in Spain) are legally constrained under PSD2 and Law 10/2010: they may not provide payment/e-money services to Spanish residents or receive settlement funds on behalf of a Spanish resident SL without a registered Spanish agency arrangement or a licensed branch filed with the Banco de España; UK EMIs that lost EU passporting rights after Brexit are therefore non-viable as a primary treasury bank. They may act only as settlement aggregators where contractually linked to a Spanish-authorised agent, and such use requires enhanced record-keeping to preserve the audit trail demanded by Spanish AML enforcement practice.

Core KYC Rejection Triggers & Defense Dossier

Statutory-minimum capital (as low as EUR 3,000) with rapid high-value turnover in the first quarters; the bank scoring engine treats fast luxury-goods revenue growth as a SEPBLAC-relevant money-laundering indicator for the watch/jewellery sector.

Root cause: Statutory-minimum capital (as low as EUR 3,000) with rapid high-value turnover in the first quarters; the bank scoring engine treats fast luxury-goods revenue growth as a SEPBLAC-relevant money-laundering indicator for the watch/jewellery sector.

Defense evidence: Escritura de constitución and Registro Mercantil certificate; NIE/TIE and foreign passports with apostille and sworn Spanish translation; detailed ISIC 4791 business plan showing the e-commerce ramp; signed platform agreements with Stripe and PayPal including merchant identification numbers and settlement terms; supplier proforma invoices and purchase orders from established EU/US watch and jewellery distribution houses; first-period VAT/Intrastat returns and customs DUA filings proving physical goods flow; IAE registration under epigraph 4791; shareholder source-of-wealth statement and prior bank reference letter.
Third-party settlement risk: aggregated payouts from Stripe/PayPal enter the operating account without an identifiable end-customer IBAN, which Spanish AML compliance units classify as third-party receipts requiring provenance proof and UBO-chain verification.

Cross-Border Clearing Corridors & Settlement Fit

Inbound equity contributions are wired by SWIFT MT103 to the SL's Spanish IBAN (format ES followed by two control digits and the 22-digit BBAN). The remittance must carry a structured reason-for-payment: 'capital contribution / aportación de capital para ampliación de capital social' for true equity, or 'shareholder loan / préstamo de socios' for debt funding. For transfers equal to or above EUR 50,000 the receiving bank captures the Banco de España statistical declaration before crediting; for amounts exceeding EUR 150,000 the bank issues an individual 'declaración de operaciones exteriores'. The corporate resolution and, where the capital is actually increased, the notarial deed of capital increase with Registro Mercantil filing must be delivered to prevent an uncommitted credit balance from being frozen as an invalid or unexplained remittance. FX conversion from USD, GBP or CHF should be pre-hedged with an FX forward or swap to lock the euro amount; no central-bank approval is required for the wiring itself. Compliance verification sequence: (1) bank receives the deed and beneficial-ownership statement; (2) bank records the non-resident shareholder's NIE/TIE and tax identification; (3) bank executes sanctions/PEP screening against the sending account; (4) after clearance, the funds are credited and, if applicable, reported as 'inversión exterior' in the Banco de España statistical model.EU suppliers are paid via SEPA Credit Transfer (SCT) using IBAN alone, with same-day settlement on the T2 layer and zero cross-border charges; the reverse-charge mechanism applies for intra-community goods. Non-EU suppliers (Swiss watch houses, USA/China jewellery manufacturers) are paid via SWIFT MT103 with the proper remittance information in field 70 identifying the invoice, purchase order and the commercial purpose (trade payment); the payment is executed at spot or against a booked FX forward where the exposure was pre-hedged. For high-value timepieces and branded gold, the prudent rail is a commercial letter of credit (sight or usance, confirmed for CHF/USD beneficiaries) opened through the Banco Santander or BBVA trade-finance desk, supported by proforma invoices, insurance certificates, weight/purity certificates for gold, and serial-number manifests for watches. Documentary collections (D/P and D/A) and low-ticket supplier settlements via the anchor bank's supply-chain finance module are permissible alternatives. The treasury should keep a dedicated multi-currency (USD, CHF, GBP) account at the anchor bank containing only working capital exposed to those currencies, with the surplus held in euro to minimise conversion friction.Outright foreign-exchange forwards (FX forward contracts) in EUR/USD and EUR/CHF to hedge imported watch and jewellery purchases, executed under the anchor bank's ISDA/CSA documentation where counterparty exposure arisesForeign-exchange swaps (fx swaps/permutas de divisas) to manage euro working-capital cycles and to bridge PSP settlement balances denominated in USD or GBPNon-deliverable forwards (NDFs) on Latin-American currencies relevant to the distribution model (EUR/ARS, EUR/MXN, EUR/UYU) where a deliverable interbank market is otherwise absent; permitted only against genuine commercial exposure and within a documented board-approved hedging policyCross-currency interest-rate swaps (CCS) used to refinance or synthetically convert shareholder loans denominated in USD/CHF into euro, protecting both coupon and amortisation cash flows against exchange-rate movementsPlain-vanilla currency options and collars (for example EUR-call/USD-put and EUR-call/CHF-put structures) purchased from tier-1 Spanish banks under EMIR clearing conventions where applicable, always supported by a documented underlying commercial exposure to avoid speculative classification

E-commerce / gateway settlement fit: Feasibility rating: MEDIUM-HIGH for Spanish-regulated electronic-money institutions and payment institutions (entidades de dinero electrónico/entidades de pago) holding a valid Banco de España licence (for example Monei, Bnext and RedSys-backed issuers); such domestic EMIs can lawfully provide IBANs, card acquiring, e-money floats and payout rails for the SL's e-commerce settlement. Their limitations are commercial rather than legal: they seldom offer meaningful FX lines, high-value watch-trade finance, commercial letters of credit, or the correspondent bank network of a tier-1 credit institution, so they should be used as secondary collection rails, not as the anchor treasury bank. Offshore digital EMIs (post-Brexit UK-licensed EMIs, Lithuanian, Polish, or other issuers without a branch in Spain) are legally constrained under PSD2 and Law 10/2010: they may not provide payment/e-money services to Spanish residents or receive settlement funds on behalf of a Spanish resident SL without a registered Spanish agency arrangement or a licensed branch filed with the Banco de España; UK EMIs that lost EU passporting rights after Brexit are therefore non-viable as a primary treasury bank. They may act only as settlement aggregators where contractually linked to a Spanish-authorised agent, and such use requires enhanced record-keeping to preserve the audit trail demanded by Spanish AML enforcement practice.

Stage 06

Corporate Tax & Transfer Pricing

Corporate income tax (CIT), box-by-box return breakdown, dividend WHT, and director personal liability.

Statutory corporate income tax (CIT)

25% general corporate income tax rate. Newly created entities and qualifying newly incorporated companies may generally apply 15% during the first tax period in which they obtain a taxable profit and the following tax period, subject to statutory conditions and exclusions.

Dividend withholding tax (WHT)

19% Spanish withholding tax on dividends paid by a Spanish company to a non-resident, subject to domestic exemptions and applicable tax treaties. The EU Parent-Subsidiary Directive exemption may eliminate withholding where the statutory conditions are satisfied, commonly including a qualifying corporate parent, minimum 5% participation or qualifying acquisition-value test, minimum one-year holding or holding commitment, subject-to-tax requirements, and anti-abuse conditions.

Mandatory Return Breakdown

Deadline: · Frequency:

File within the 25 calendar days following the six-month period after the end of the tax year. For a calendar-year company closing on 31 December, the normal filing window is 1 July through 25 July of the following year. If the final day is not a business day, the applicable electronic filing rules extend the deadline to the next business day.

Deadline: · Frequency:

Installments are generally payable during the first twenty calendar days of April, October, and December. The relevant calculation method is normally based either on the prior year's final tax liability or on the current-period taxable base, depending on statutory eligibility and mandatory-method rules.

Deadline: · Frequency:

Generally filed during the month following the ten-month period after the end of the tax period. For a 31 December year-end, the normal deadline is 30 November of the following year.

Box-by-Box Return Breakdown (non-resident focus)

Corporate identification and tax-period fields Enter the company tax identification number (NIF), legal name, registered address, tax period, financial year dates, legal form, and filing type, including original, substitute, or supplementary filing. A non-resident shareholder does not file these fields for the Spanish SL. The Spanish SL files using its own NIF. The non-resident shareholder must maintain its foreign tax identification and Spanish tax-representation documentation where required. Failure or incorrect filing may generate administrative penalties generally ranging from 50% to 150% of the unpaid amount, subject to culpability, concealment, and repeated-offense rules. Electronic filing failures may also be treated as filing failures.

Use current-period figures only where the company is legally required or entitled to use that method; document exceptional transactions and group reorganizations affecting the calculation. Failure to file, late filing, or materially incorrect information may trigger fixed or proportional penalties under Spain's General Tax Law, with increased exposure where the omission prevents or obstructs tax administration or conceals related-party income.

Failure to file, late filing, or materially incorrect information may trigger fixed or proportional penalties under Spain's General Tax Law, with increased exposure where the omission prevents or obstructs tax administration or conceals related-party income.

Failure to file, late filing, or materially incorrect information may trigger fixed or proportional penalties under Spain's General Tax Law, with increased exposure where the omission prevents or obstructs tax administration or conceals related-party income.

Obtain current jurisdiction classification before filing. Treaty residence alone does not eliminate reporting where specific anti-abuse or non-cooperative-jurisdiction rules apply. Failure to file, late filing, or materially incorrect information may trigger fixed or proportional penalties under Spain's General Tax Law, with increased exposure where the omission prevents or obstructs tax administration or conceals related-party income.

Transfer Pricing & Economic Substance

Master / Local File threshold: Spain generally requires related-party transaction documentation, subject to statutory content and exemptions, unless the aggregate value of transactions with the same related person during the tax period does not exceed EUR 250,000 at arm's length, with important exclusions and special rules for transactions involving real estate, intangible assets, securities, or specified tax regimes. A Master File is generally required for Spanish entities belonging to a group with consolidated net turnover of at least EUR 45 million. A Country-by-Country Report generally applies to multinational groups with consolidated revenue of at least EUR 750 million and is normally filed by the ultimate parent or designated surrogate entity. The relevant local-currency threshold is EUR 250,000 for the principal small-transaction documentation exemption.

Economic substance scope: Spain has no separate UAE-style or standalone generic Economic Substance Regulations regime. Economic substance is nevertheless material under the Corporate Income Tax Law, transfer-pricing rules, beneficial-ownership principles, anti-abuse provisions, controlled foreign company rules, the EU Anti-Tax Avoidance Directive framework, treaty principal-purpose tests, and permanent-establishment rules. A Spanish SL conducting online jewelry and watch sales should maintain genuine Spanish functions, personnel or outsourced operational capacity, inventory or logistics control where claimed, decision-making, commercial risk, customer management, payment controls, and adequate capitalization. Conduit financing, royalty pass-throughs, artificial management charges, circular payments, and profit allocation inconsistent with actual functions are high-risk.

Fatal Compliance Red Lines & Director Liability

Corporate income tax evasion

Statutory sanction: Criminal tax fraud generally carries imprisonment of 1 to 5 years and a fine of 1 to 6 times the amount defrauded, together with loss of public subsidies and tax benefits for a period of 3 to 6 years. Aggravated cases may carry imprisonment of 2 to 6 years and a fine of 2 to 6 times the amount defrauded.

Director personal liability: Directors and de facto managers who knowingly participate may incur criminal liability, civil restitution for unpaid tax and damages, disqualification, and confiscation. Travel restrictions are not automatic but may be imposed judicially in criminal proceedings. Imprisonment is possible only where the statutory criminal elements are established.
VAT fraud and undeclared ecommerce sales

Statutory sanction: Administrative penalties may include fixed penalties and proportional penalties commonly ranging from 50% to 150% of the unpaid tax, plus interest and surcharges. Criminal liability may arise where the tax-fraud threshold is exceeded or organized fraud is established.

Director personal liability: Directors may be jointly or subsidiarily liable under the General Tax Law where they caused or failed to prevent the infringement, particularly during dissolution or non-compliance. Criminal participation can result in imprisonment, fines, restitution, and asset measures.
False invoicing and sham expenses

Statutory sanction: Disallowance of the expense, reassessment of corporate income tax and VAT, late-payment interest, and penalties generally based on the unpaid tax. False-document conduct may also constitute a criminal offense when connected with tax fraud or accounting falsification.

Director personal liability: Directors, accountants, and authorized signatories may face civil recovery, administrative liability, professional sanctions, and criminal prosecution where they knowingly created or used false records.
Transfer-pricing manipulation

Statutory sanction: The AEAT may make a primary adjustment, impose compensating adjustments, deny deductions, apply withholding tax, charge interest, and impose transfer-pricing documentation or valuation penalties. Failure to provide required documentation can attract penalties based on transaction value or fixed statutory amounts.

Director personal liability: Directors may incur subsidiary tax liability where the company cannot pay and the statutory conditions are met. Deliberate profit diversion may support criminal tax-fraud allegations and civil claims by the company or creditors.
Withholding-tax failure

Statutory sanction: The Spanish payer may be assessed for the unpaid withholding, late-payment interest, and administrative penalties. The foreign recipient may also face Spanish non-resident tax exposure where treaty or domestic relief is unavailable.

Director personal liability: Directors may face subsidiary liability for knowingly approving non-compliant payments or failing to maintain withholding controls. Criminal liability requires additional statutory elements such as intentional tax fraud above the criminal threshold.
Customs, origin, and counterfeit-goods violations

Statutory sanction: Consequences may include customs debt, seizure, forfeiture, destruction of goods, administrative fines, loss of customs simplifications, trademark damages, and criminal prosecution for serious intellectual-property or customs offenses.

Director personal liability: Directors and responsible officers may face civil damages, confiscation, and criminal fines or imprisonment where intentional counterfeiting, smuggling, or aggravated customs fraud is established.
Anti-money-laundering and suspicious-payment activity

Statutory sanction: Under Spanish AML legislation, serious and very serious infringements can result in substantial corporate fines, potentially up to EUR 5 million or 10% of annual turnover for serious cases and up to EUR 10 million or 10% of annual turnover for very serious cases, together with public reprimand, authorization consequences, and management disqualification. Cash payments involving a business or professional are generally restricted above EUR 1,000; the limit is generally EUR 10,000 where the payer is a non-resident individual not acting as a business or professional.

Director personal liability: Managers and officers may receive personal fines, temporary disqualification, and civil liability. Criminal money-laundering liability may involve imprisonment, fines, confiscation, and judicial measures. Travel bans are not automatic and require judicial or statutory authority.
Shell company and beneficial-ownership concealment

Statutory sanction: Potential consequences include denial of treaty and participation exemptions, controlled foreign company or anti-abuse adjustments, tax reassessment, AML penalties, beneficial-owner reporting breaches, and criminal liability for fraud, money laundering, or document falsification where applicable.

Director personal liability: Directors and de facto controllers may face civil restitution, tax liability, asset confiscation, disqualification, and imprisonment if criminal offenses are proven. The corporate veil is not automatically pierced solely because the entity is closely held.
Accounting, books, and corporate-record falsification

Statutory sanction: Possible consequences include rejection of tax deductions, accounting penalties, tax reassessment, refusal of insolvency protection, commercial-register consequences, and criminal accounting or document offenses.

Director personal liability: Directors may incur civil liability to the company, shareholders, creditors, and tax authorities, as well as criminal fines or imprisonment where intentional falsification or insolvency-related misconduct is established.
Insolvency and creditor prejudice

Statutory sanction: Potential consequences include clawback, insolvency disqualification, director liability for the insolvency deficit, damages, asset recovery, and criminal insolvency offenses in aggravated cases.

Director personal liability: Directors may be ordered to cover all or part of the insolvency deficit, return transferred assets, pay civil damages, and bear criminal fines or imprisonment. Judicial travel restrictions may be imposed in insolvency or criminal proceedings where legally justified.
